results.name: singleton_adjacent_up_minus_down
results.description: On single-example sets, yes-rate to targets 1-3 above the example minus yes-rate to targets 1-3 below it; observed above null means the top-marking model's downward-only generalization from one example is too strong right next to the example (people extend upward more), below null means it is too weak.
results.code:
# name: singleton_adjacent_up_minus_down
# description: On single-example sets, yes-rate to targets 1-3 above the example minus yes-rate to targets 1-3 below it; observed above null means the top-marking model's downward-only generalization from one example is too strong right next to the example (people extend upward more), below null means it is too weak.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    single = ~sets.str.contains(",")
    x = pd.to_numeric(sets.where(single, "0"), errors="coerce").fillna(0).to_numpy()
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    d = t - x
    single = single.to_numpy()
    up = single & (d >= 1) & (d <= 3)
    dn = single & (d <= -1) & (d >= -3)
    if up.sum() == 0 or dn.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[up].mean() - r[dn].mean())

results.name: previous_examples_carryover
results.description: Yes-rate on non-example targets that were an example in the immediately preceding trial's set (same session, consecutive trial_index) minus the yes-rate on other non-example targets; observed above null means examples from the previous trial leak into the current concept (cross-trial contamination the trial-independent model cannot produce).
results.code:
# name: previous_examples_carryover
# description: Yes-rate on non-example targets that were an example in the immediately preceding trial's set (same session, consecutive trial_index) minus the yes-rate on other non-example targets; observed above null means examples from the previous trial leak into the current concept (cross-trial contamination the trial-independent model cannot produce).
def test_statistic(df):
    ti = df["trial_index"].to_numpy()
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.replace(" ", "")
    s = ("," + sets + ",").to_numpy()
    t = df["target"].astype(int).astype(str).to_numpy()
    tok = np.array(["," + a + "," for a in t])
    prev_s = np.concatenate([[""], s[:-1]])
    consec = np.concatenate([[False], np.diff(ti) == 1])
    non_ex = np.array([a not in b for a, b in zip(tok, s)])
    in_prev = np.array([a in b for a, b in zip(tok, prev_s)]) & consec & (prev_s != s)
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    a = non_ex & in_prev
    b = non_ex & ~in_prev
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: target_100_yes_rate
results.description: Yes-rate when the target is 100 and 100 is not among the examples; observed below null means the model over-credits ranges/rules reaching the domain's top (e.g. decade-aligned ranges ending at 100), above null means people treat 100 as more salient than the model.

results.name: first_encounter_minus_later_yes
results.description: Within each session (inferred from trial_index resets), yes-rate on non-example targets for the first two trials on which a given example set appears minus the yes-rate on that set's later trials in the session; observed above null means people narrow a set's concept with repeated exposure (below null: broaden), an exposure dynamic the static model lacks.
results.code:
# name: first_encounter_minus_later_yes
# description: Within each session (inferred from trial_index resets), yes-rate on non-example targets for the first two trials on which a given example set appears minus the yes-rate on that set's later trials in the session; observed above null means people narrow a set's concept with repeated exposure (below null: broaden), an exposure dynamic the static model lacks.
def test_statistic(df):
    ti = df["trial_index"].to_numpy()
    sess = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(np.diff(ti) < 0)])
    key = pd.Series(sess.astype(str)) + "|" + df["number_set"].astype(str).reset_index(drop=True)
    occ = key.groupby(key).cumcount().to_numpy()
    t = df["target"].astype(int).astype(str).to_numpy()
    s = ("," + df["number_set"].astype(str).str.replace(" ", "") + ",").to_numpy()
    non_ex = np.array([("," + a + ",") not in b for a, b in zip(t, s)])
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    early = non_ex & (occ < 2)
    late = non_ex & (occ >= 2)
    if early.sum() == 0 or late.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[early].mean() - r[late].mean())

results.name: session_yes_rate_sd
results.description: Standard deviation across sessions (inferred from trial_index resetting to a lower value) of each session's overall yes-rate; observed above null means participants differ in their overall willingness to say "yes" far more than the single-population model (no individual differences) produces.
results.code:
# name: session_yes_rate_sd
# description: Standard deviation across sessions (inferred from trial_index resetting to a lower value) of each session's overall yes-rate; observed above null means participants differ in their overall willingness to say "yes" far more than the single-population model (no individual differences) produces.
def test_statistic(df):
    ti = df["trial_index"].to_numpy()
    sess = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(np.diff(ti) < 0)])
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    counts = np.bincount(sess)
    means = np.bincount(sess, weights=r) / np.maximum(counts, 1)
    means = means[counts > 0]
    if len(means) < 2:
        return 0.0
    return float(np.std(means))

results.name: session_example_yes_sd
results.description: Standard deviation across sessions (inferred from trial_index resets) of the yes-rate on trials whose target is one of the shown examples; observed above null means some participants reject trivially consistent targets much more than others (participant-specific noise/lapse heterogeneity the model lacks).
results.code:
# name: session_example_yes_sd
# description: Standard deviation across sessions (inferred from trial_index resets) of the yes-rate on trials whose target is one of the shown examples; observed above null means some participants reject trivially consistent targets much more than others (participant-specific noise/lapse heterogeneity the model lacks).
def test_statistic(df):
    ti = df["trial_index"].to_numpy()
    sess = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(np.diff(ti) < 0)])
    t = df["target"].astype(int).astype(str)
    s = "," + df["number_set"].astype(str).str.replace(" ", "") + ","
    is_ex = np.array([("," + a + ",") in b for a, b in zip(t, s)])
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    if is_ex.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    counts = np.bincount(sess[is_ex], minlength=sess.max() + 1)
    sums = np.bincount(sess[is_ex], weights=r[is_ex], minlength=sess.max() + 1)
    ok = counts >= 3
    if ok.sum() < 2:
        return 0.0
    return float(np.std(sums[ok] / counts[ok]))

results.name: large_gap_interior_yes
results.description: On sets of >=2 examples whose largest gap between consecutive sorted examples is >=30, yes-rate to non-example targets inside that gap and >=10 from both of its ends; observed above null means people fill in between distant example clusters (one wide range) more than the model, below null means they treat the clusters as separate more than the model.

results.name: dense_minus_sparse_upward
results.description: Yes-rate to targets 1-10 above the largest example on sets of >=3 examples minus the same on single-example sets; the model predicts top-marking credit fades with more examples (so this is positive), so observed below null means people's upward generalization does not recover with denser sets as much as the model claims, above null means it recovers more.
results.code:
# name: dense_minus_sparse_upward
# description: Yes-rate to targets 1-10 above the largest example on sets of >=3 examples minus the same on single-example sets; the model predicts top-marking credit fades with more examples (so this is positive), so observed below null means people's upward generalization does not recover with denser sets as much as the model claims, above null means it recovers more.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.replace(" ", "")
    n = sets.str.count(",").to_numpy() + 1
    lut = {k: max(int(z) for z in k.split(",")) for k in sets.unique()}
    mx = sets.map(lut).to_numpy()
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    d = t - mx
    above = (d >= 1) & (d <= 10)
    a = above & (n >= 3)
    b = above & (n == 1)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())
